questions.q: Around which year is the last Maurya emperor generally accepted to have been assassinated?
questions.a: Around 185 BCE, by his commander-in-chief Pushyamitra Shunga.

questions.q: Who assassinated the last Maurya emperor?
questions.a: Pushyamitra Shunga, the emperor's commander-in-chief, who then founded the Shunga dynasty.

questions.q:
Match each term in Column I with its meaning in Column II.
Column I: 1. Matrimonial alliance  2. Tributary kingdom  3. Age of reorganisation  4. Border areas
Column II: P. A name some scholars give to the period after the Maurya empire  Q. A kingdom that had been under the overlordship of the Maurya empire  R. An alliance between two kingdoms cemented by a marriage in their royal families  S. Lands that kings constantly wrestled over to keep their kingdom safe from attacks
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: Matrimonial alliance = an alliance cemented by a royal marriage; tributary kingdom = one that had been under Maurya overlordship; age of reorganisation = the scholars' name for the post-Maurya period; border areas = lands kings wrestled over to keep the kingdom safe.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the age of reorganisation there was constant wrestling between kingdoms for control over areas along their borders.
Reason (R): Gaining control over border areas was important to keep a kingdom safe from attacks.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: kings fought over border areas because holding them kept the kingdom safe from attacks.

questions.q: Give two results of the breakup of the Maurya empire that the chapter mentions.
questions.a: Many new kingdoms emerged across the subcontinent, often earlier tributary kingdoms of the Maurya empire; and the northwest became weak, which exposed it to invasions from outside the subcontinent.
s: States that many new kingdoms emerged, often the earlier tributary kingdoms
States that the northwest became weak and open to invasions from outside

questions.q: True or False? 'According to the chapter, the Kushanas were one of the dynasties from within the subcontinent.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The chapter lists the Kushanas, together with the Indo-Greeks and the Shakas, among the dynasties from outside the subcontinent.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: the Kushanas, like the Indo-Greeks and Shakas, came from outside the subcontinent

questions.q: The chapter says that, together with the political events of this age, there was a burst in the development of art, architecture and literature. Give one example of such work from each of these dynasties: (a) the Shungas (b) the Satavahanas (c) the Chedis.
questions.a: (a) Shungas: the carved railings and reliefs of the Buddha's life added to the Bharhut Stupa. (b) Satavahanas: the Karla caves for Buddhist monks, or the yaksha carved at Pitalkhora. (c) Chedis: the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves near Bhubaneswar, or the Hathigumpha inscription.
s: Gives a correct Shunga example, such as the Bharhut railings and reliefs
Gives a correct Satavahana example, such as the Karla caves or the Pitalkhora yaksha
Gives a correct Chedi example, such as the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves

questions.q: The chapter's chart of prominent dynasties (Fig. 6.3) lists six dynasties from within the subcontinent (Shungas, Chedis, Satavahanas, Cholas, Cheras, Pandyas) and three from outside it (Indo-Greeks, Shakas, Kushanas). (a) What fraction of the nine dynasties came from outside? (b) Through which region did the invaders enter, and why was it open to them after the Mauryas? (c) Give one example of an outside dynasty taking up local culture. (d) A student says, 'Since most dynasties were from within, foreign invasions hardly mattered to the reorganisation.' Judge this claim.
questions.a: (a) 3 of 9, that is one-third. (b) The northwest frontier; after the breakup of the Maurya empire the northwest became weak, exposing it to invasions. (c) For example, the Indo-Greek ambassador Heliodorus praised Vasudeva as the 'god of gods' (or Indo-Greek coins showing Vasudeva-Krishna and Lakshmi, or Kanishka's coins showing Shiva and Nandi). (d) The claim is wrong: the chapter's summary says internal conflicts were coupled with foreign invasions, and together they led to the reorganisation of political powers; a count of dynasties does not measure how much each changed the map, and the outsiders ruled large areas of the northwest, north and centre.
s: Finds the fraction: 3 of 9 = one-third
Names the northwest and explains it was weak after the Maurya breakup
Gives a correct example of an outside dynasty taking up local culture
Rejects the claim using the summary that internal conflicts and foreign invasions together led to the reorganisation

questions.q: One of the chapter's Big Questions asks what values or principles guided the rulers of this period. Use evidence from four different dynasties to show how each ruler treated schools of thought other than his own, and then judge whether protecting all schools of thought was a common principle of the age.
questions.a: Shungas: they revived Vedic rituals, yet other schools of thought continued to flourish. Satavahanas: devout followers of Vasudeva, but they granted tax-free agricultural land to Vedic scholars, Jaina and Buddhist monks. Chedis: Kharavela, a devoted follower of Jain teachings, called himself a 'respector of every sect and repairer of every temple'. Pandyas: their inscriptions assert concern for their subjects' welfare and encouragement to all schools of thought and belief. Judgement: yes, across north, Deccan, east and south, rulers with their own faiths extended protection to all schools, which the chapter calls a fundamental part of the 'Indian ethos'.
s: Shunga evidence: Vedic revival while other schools still flourished
Satavahana evidence: followers of Vasudeva who gave tax-free land to Vedic scholars, Jaina and Buddhist monks
Chedi evidence: Kharavela, a Jain, as respector of every sect and repairer of every temple
Pandya evidence: inscriptions showing encouragement to all schools of thought (or another correct fourth dynasty)
Gives a reasoned judgement that this was a common principle, the 'Indian ethos'

questions.q: Which work was compiled by Patanjali during the Shunga period?
questions.a: The Yoga Sutras, compiled by Patanjali in this period.

questions.q: The Bharhut Stupa, which presents beautiful examples of Shunga art, is in which present-day state?
questions.a: Madhya Pradesh.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Shungas.
I. The Shunga empire under Pushyamitra was larger than the Maurya empire before it.
II. After some initial military campaign against the Greeks, Pushyamitra maintained friendly relations with them.
III. The Bharhut Stupa was probably built during Ashoka's time, and the Shungas added carved railings and reliefs to it.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements II and III are correct. Statement I is wrong: Pushyamitra's empire was smaller than the Maurya empire.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The carved railings and reliefs at the Bharhut Stupa are considered some of the earliest examples of Buddhist art.
Reason (R): Pushyamitra Shunga performed the ashvamedha yajna to establish himself as a most powerful ruler.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: a Vedic ritual performed by the king does not explain why the Bharhut carvings count among the earliest Buddhist art.

questions.q: (a) Name two things shown in the carvings on the railings of the Bharhut Stupa. (b) Why are these carvings important for the history of Buddhist art?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: Lakshmi, a group of singers and dancers, elephants holding up the wheel of dharma, stories from the Buddha's life. (b) They are considered some of the earliest examples of Buddhist art.
s: Names two carvings shown, such as Lakshmi, singers and dancers, or elephants with the wheel of dharma
States that they are among the earliest examples of Buddhist art

questions.q: True or False? 'The Shunga dynasty ruled over the far south of India, around Madurai.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The Shungas ruled over parts of north and central India; Madurai was the capital of the Pandyas in the south.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: the Shungas ruled parts of north and central India, while Madurai was the Pandya capital

questions.q: Answer briefly. (a) Who founded the Shunga dynasty, and over which parts of India did it rule? (b) Which Vedic ritual did he perform to establish himself as a most powerful ruler? (c) Which language emerged as one of the preferred languages for philosophical and literary works in this period?
questions.a: (a) Pushyamitra Shunga; parts of north and central India. (b) The ashvamedha yajna. (c) Sanskrit.
s: Names Pushyamitra Shunga and north and central India
Names the ashvamedha yajna
Names Sanskrit

questions.q: Compare the Shungas and the Satavahanas on four points, writing one line for each dynasty under each point: (a) the region they ruled, (b) their attitude to schools of thought, (c) one contribution to art or architecture, (d) how their rule came to an end or how long it lasted.
questions.a: (a) Shungas: parts of north and central India; Satavahanas: large parts of the Deccan, mostly present-day Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Maharashtra. (b) Shungas: Vedic rituals revived while other schools continued to flourish; Satavahanas: followers of Vasudeva who granted tax-free land to Vedic scholars, Jaina and Buddhist monks. (c) Shungas: carved railings and reliefs at the Bharhut Stupa; Satavahanas: the Karla caves or the Pitalkhora yaksha. (d) Shungas: gone about a century after Pushyamitra; Satavahanas: ruled from the 2nd century BCE and fragmented in the 3rd century CE because of weak central control and economic decline.
s: Compares the regions: north and central India against the Deccan
Compares attitudes: Vedic revival with other schools flourishing against Vasudeva followers who gave land to all
Compares art: Bharhut railings against Karla caves or Pitalkhora yaksha
Compares the end: Shunga rule gone a century later against Satavahana fragmentation in the 3rd century CE

questions.q: Which were the two most famous capitals of the Satavahanas?
questions.a: Amravati and Pratishthana (Paithan).

questions.q: A Satavahana coin carries a Brahmi inscription that reads 'King Lord Satakarni, son of Gautami'. Which Satavahana practice does this inscription best show?
o: Princes were often named after their mothers
Kings were named after the gods they followed
Kings took the name of their capital city
Princes were named after their teachers
questions.a: In the Satavahana tradition princes were often named after their mothers: Gautamiputra Satakarni was named after his mother, Gautami Balashri.

questions.q:
Match each Satavahana-period site in Column I with what the chapter says about it in Column II.
Column I: 1. Karla caves  2. Naneghat caves  3. Pitalkhora caves  4. Nashik
Column II: P. A yaksha carved by Kanhadasa, a goldsmith  Q. An important inscription of Gautami Balashri  R. Caves near Lonavala made for Buddhist monks, with a stone replica of a stupa  S. Caves near Pune used to collect tolls and as resting places for traders
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: Karla = caves near Lonavala for Buddhist monks; Naneghat = toll collection and resting place for traders near Pune; Pitalkhora = the yaksha made by Kanhadasa the goldsmith; Nashik = Gautami Balashri's important inscription.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Coins issued by the Satavahana rulers have been found in regions from Gujarat to Andhra Pradesh.
Reason (R): The Satavahanas were devout followers of Vasudeva.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: the kings' religious devotion does not explain where their coins are found; the spread of the coins goes with the kingdom's trade.

questions.q: (a) After whom was Gautamiputra Satakarni named? (b) Give one sign from the chapter that his mother had influence in the kingdom.
questions.a: (a) After his mother, Gautami Balashri, since Satavahana princes were often named after their mothers. (b) She donated land to Buddhist monks and had an important inscription carved at Nashik.
s: Names his mother, Gautami Balashri
Gives a sign of her influence: land donated to Buddhist monks or the Nashik inscription

questions.q: A Satavahana king is a devout follower of Vasudeva (Krishna). In the same year he grants tax-free agricultural land to a Vedic scholar, a Jaina monk and a Buddhist monk. (a) How does such a grant help the people who receive it? (b) What do the three grants together show about how this king used his power, beyond his own faith?
questions.a: (a) The land is farmland on which no tax has to be paid, so it supports the scholars and monks and helps them pursue their studies and practices. (b) Although he followed Vasudeva himself, he supported other schools of thought too, so under his rule those schools could flourish; his patronage was not limited to his own belief.
s: Explains that tax-free land supports the receivers so they can pursue their studies and practices
Infers that the king patronised other schools of thought, not only his own faith

questions.q: The Satavahana empire fragmented into smaller independent kingdoms in the 3rd century CE. (a) Name the factors the chapter gives as the most significant. (b) Explain why weak central control could break up a large kingdom. (c) What did the breakup pave the way for?
questions.a: (a) Weak central control and a gradual economic decline. (b) When the centre cannot hold its regions together, local rulers can stop obeying and set up their own kingdoms. (c) It paved the way for regional powers to assert or reassert their dominance and establish new kingdoms.
s: Names weak central control and gradual economic decline
Explains how weak central control lets regions break away
States that regional powers asserted themselves and set up new kingdoms

questions.q:
The ashvamedha yajna appears twice in the chapter: Pushyamitra Shunga performed it, and the Naneghat inscriptions record that a Satavahana widow queen performed it among several Vedic rituals. A student claims: 'Only a king who had just founded a new dynasty would perform the ashvamedha.'
(a) Using the chapter, state whether Pushyamitra fits the claim, and why he performed the ritual.
(b) Does the Satavahana case fit the claim? Give two ways in which it does not.
(c) Decide whether the claim holds, and state what the two cases together show about Vedic rituals in this age.
questions.a: (a) Yes: Pushyamitra founded the Shunga dynasty and performed the ashvamedha to establish himself as a most powerful ruler. (b) No: the performer was a queen, not a king, and she was a widow queen of the already ruling Satavahana dynasty, not the founder of a new one. (c) The claim does not hold, because one of the only two cases in the chapter breaks it; together they show that Vedic rituals were being revived and performed by different dynasties in different regions (north and central India, and the Deccan), even by a royal woman.
s: States that Pushyamitra fits: he founded the Shunga dynasty and performed it to establish himself as a most powerful ruler
Gives two mismatches: a queen, not a king, and not the founder of a new dynasty
Rejects the claim and concludes that Vedic rituals were revived across dynasties and regions

questions.q:
A play shows a trader of the Satavahana age. On his way to the coast he passes caves cut into a hillside near Pune, close to a major trade route, where he pays toll and rests for the night. His carts carry 50 bales of textiles, 30 sacks of spices and 20 logs of sandalwood for ships bound for the Roman Empire. He returns with 12 crates of glass and 8 jars of perfumed ointment. In the play the toll is 1 coin for every 10 units of goods, on each trip.
(a) Name the caves where he pays toll.
(b) How many coins of toll does he pay in all, going and returning?
(c) Which of his goods were imports?
(d) A minister in the play wants to double the toll to fill the treasury. Give one argument for and one against, using what the chapter says about the kingdom's wealth.
questions.a: (a) The Naneghat caves. (b) Going: 50 + 30 + 20 = 100 units, 10 coins; returning: 12 + 8 = 20 units, 2 coins; 12 coins in all. (c) Glass and perfumed ointment. (d) For: tolls and taxes on trade added revenue to the kingdom. Against: the kingdom's prosperity rested on active trade networks, so a heavy toll could discourage traders and shrink that trade.
s: Names the Naneghat caves
Computes 10 + 2 = 12 coins
Names glass and perfumed ointment as imports
Gives one argument for (tolls add revenue) and one against (trade was the source of prosperity)

questions.q: Prepare a fact file on the Satavahanas with one correct fact under each heading. (a) Region ruled (b) Two capitals (c) Two goods exported (d) Their faith and the schools they supported (e) Their naming tradition, with an example
questions.a: (a) Large parts of the Deccan, mostly present-day Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Maharashtra. (b) Amravati and Pratishthana (Paithan). (c) Any two of spices, textiles, sandalwood, gold-plated pearls, ivory. (d) Devout followers of Vasudeva (Krishna) who granted tax-free land to Vedic scholars, Jaina and Buddhist monks. (e) Princes were often named after their mothers, as Gautamiputra Satakarni was named after Gautami Balashri.
s: Region: the Deccan, mainly Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Maharashtra
Capitals: Amravati and Pratishthana (Paithan)
Two correct exports, such as spices and sandalwood
Faith: Vasudeva, with land grants to Vedic scholars, Jaina and Buddhist monks
Naming after mothers, with Gautamiputra Satakarni as the example

questions.q: In which script is the Hathigumpha inscription of King Kharavela written?
questions.a: Brahmi script.

questions.q: Kharavela of Kalinga was sometimes called by which title?
questions.a: Bhikshu-raja, the monk-king, because he was a devoted follower of Jain teachings.

questions.q: After the decline of the Maurya Empire, Kalinga rose as a prominent power under the kings of which dynasty?
questions.a: The Chedi dynasty, whose main rulers included Kharavela.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): After the decline of the Maurya Empire, Kalinga rose as a prominent power.
Reason (R): Kharavela invaded the southern region and brought the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas under his rule.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: Kalinga did rise under the Chedi kings, but Kharavela does not seem to have invaded the southern region; the location of his claimed battle against south Indian kings is unknown.

questions.q: (a) From the chapter's description of the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves, what is 'rock-cut architecture'? (b) Which site in Kalinga does the chapter give as a notable example of it?
questions.a: (a) Architecture in which rooms, panels and statues are carved out of the rock itself, as in these caves, rather than built up from separate pieces. (b) The Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves near Bhubaneswar.
s: Explains that rooms, panels and statues are carved out of the rock
Names the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves near Bhubaneswar

questions.q: True or False? 'Kharavela proudly declares in his inscription that he created a council of ascetics and sages from a hundred regions.' Give the verdict and what this tells us about him.
questions.a: True. The Hathigumpha inscription says so; it shows that, though a Jain, he took pride in extending his protection to all schools of thought.
s: States the verdict: True
Explains that it shows he protected and respected all schools of thought

questions.q: Answer briefly. (a) Near which city are the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves? (b) For whom were they likely developed? (c) Which inscription is prominently displayed in one of these caves, and what does it record?
questions.a: (a) Near Bhubaneswar. (b) For Jain monks. (c) The Hathigumpha inscription, which records King Kharavela's accomplishments year after year, including his military campaigns and his works for the welfare of his people.
s: Names Bhubaneswar
States that they were likely for Jain monks
Names the Hathigumpha inscription and says it records Kharavela's year-by-year achievements

questions.q:
The chapter shows three things from the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves near Bhubaneswar: the caves themselves, with panels, statues and spacious rooms carved into the rock; the Hathigumpha inscription in Brahmi script; and a carved panel showing a scene from the Ramayana (Fig. 6.13.3).
(a) What do the design and craftsmanship of the caves tell a historian about Kalinga at this time?
(b) Kharavela was sometimes called bhikshu-raja, or monk-king. Why was he given this title, and what does the chapter say that stops us from thinking he cared only for his own faith?
(c) What does the carved Ramayana panel show a historian about the stories known to the people who made these caves?
(d) A classmate describes Kharavela only as a conqueror, from his military campaigns. What else does the Hathigumpha inscription record that changes this picture?
questions.a: (a) Kalinga had highly skilled craftsmen who could carve intricate panels, statues and spacious rooms out of the rock, making the caves notable examples of rock-cut architecture. (b) He was a devoted follower of Jain teachings, hence monk-king; but the chapter says he respected all schools of thought, so his title tells us his own faith, not that he ignored others. (c) A scene from the Ramayana was carved there, so the Ramayana story was known in Kalinga at this time and was thought worth carving in stone. (d) Besides his victorious military campaigns, it records his benevolent works for the welfare of his people, so he was also a ruler who worked for his subjects, not only a conqueror.
s: Infers that Kalinga had highly skilled craftsmen able to carve rock-cut architecture
Links bhikshu-raja to his Jain devotion and notes that he respected all schools of thought
Infers that the Ramayana story was known in Kalinga and carved in stone
Adds his benevolent works for the welfare of his people to the picture of a conqueror

questions.q: Which city was the capital of the Pandya kingdom?
questions.a: Madurai.

questions.q: A student's poster on Chera trade lists four goods the Chera kingdom exported to the Roman Empire and West Asia. Which one should be removed because the chapter names it as an import of the Satavahanas, not a Chera export?
questions.a: Glass: the Satavahanas imported glass and perfumed ointments, while the Cheras exported spices, timber, ivory and pearls.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the south in this age.
I. The Cholas ruled parts of south India from the 3rd century BCE to the 13th century CE.
II. Sangam poetry mainly records the dates of battles and the names of kings.
III. The Cheras had extensive trade connections with the Roman Empire and West Asia.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements I and III are correct. Statement II is wrong: Sangam poetry mainly expresses personal emotions such as love and societal values like heroism and generosity.

questions.q: True or False? 'The Pandyas were only a land power, and their trade stayed within the subcontinent.' Give the verdict and two facts from the chapter that support it.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the Pandyas were an important naval power of the subcontinent, and Megasthenes, in his Indika, describes the kingdom as involved in active trade with distant powers like the Greeks and Romans, apart from much internal trade.
s: States the verdict: False
Gives both facts: an important naval power, and active trade with the Greeks and Romans (Megasthenes)

questions.q: Pearls appear three times in the chapter: among the Satavahanas' trade goods, among the Cheras' exports, and in Kharavela's claim that hundreds of pearls were brought to him from the Pandya kingdom. Explain what each of the three mentions tells a historian about trade in this age.
questions.a: Satavahanas: luxury items like gold-plated pearls were part of trade networks reaching as far as the Roman Empire. Cheras: their kingdom was a hub for exporting pearls, with spices, timber and ivory, to the Roman Empire and West Asia. Kharavela and the Pandyas: there was internal trade too, as pearls from the far south reached Kalinga in the east.
s: Satavahana mention: pearls were part of long-distance trade reaching Rome
Chera mention: the kingdom was a hub exporting pearls to Rome and West Asia
Kharavela mention: pearls show internal trade from the Pandya south to Kalinga

questions.q: Tell the story of the Silappadikaram, the Tale of the Anklet, in four steps. (a) Where did Kannagi and Kovalan first live happily? (b) Why did they travel to Madurai? (c) What happened to Kovalan in Madurai? (d) How did Kannagi prove his innocence, and what happened to the king?
questions.a: (a) In the prosperous Chola capital city of Puhar. (b) Kovalan had lost all his wealth over a dancer; Kannagi forgave him and they went to Madurai, the Pandya capital, hoping to rebuild their lives. (c) He was falsely accused of theft while selling one of Kannagi's anklets and was executed by the Pandya king. (d) She revealed her second anklet; the king, realising his mistake, died of shock.
s: Names Puhar, the Chola capital
Explains they went to Madurai to rebuild their lives after Kovalan lost his wealth
States that Kovalan was falsely accused of theft and executed
States that Kannagi showed her second anklet and the king died of shock

questions.q:
A school is planning a 'Sangam Day' exhibition and can feature only ONE southern kingdom. The planning notes read: Kingdom X, capital Uraiyur: the heroine of the Silappadikaram first lived happily in its prosperous city of Puhar. Kingdom Y, capital Vanji: its rulers encouraged the growth of Tamil literature. Kingdom Z, capital Madurai: the same epic's trial of Kovalan and the death of its king take place here. The organisers' rule is strict: the exhibit must be about a kingdom the chapter says supported the Sangam poets, not about works composed later.
(a) Name kingdoms X, Y and Z.
(b) What does the word 'sangam' refer to in 'Sangam literature'?
(c) Why do the notes on X and Z not meet the organisers' rule, even though both are linked to a famous Tamil work?
(d) Which kingdom should the school feature? Decide, and support your choice with one fact from the chapter that is not in the notes.
questions.a: (a) X = Cholas, Y = Cheras, Z = Pandyas. (b) An assembly of poets; the word comes from the Sanskrit sangha, meaning association or coming together. (c) Both links come from the Silappadikaram, which was composed soon after the Sangam collections, so it is a later epic and not one of the Sangam poems. (d) The Cheras (Y): besides encouraging Tamil literature, the chapter says they patronised Sangam poets, which is exactly the support for Sangam poets the rule asks for; the chapter says this of no other kingdom.
s: Identifies X as Cholas, Y as Cheras and Z as Pandyas
Explains that sangam refers to an assembly of poets
Explains that the Silappadikaram was composed after the Sangam collections, so it is not Sangam poetry
Chooses the Cheras and adds that they patronised Sangam poets

questions.q:
Explain how the Chola king Karikala's Kallanai (Grand Anicut) led to the Kaveri delta being called the 'rice bowl of the South', and judge its value today.
(a) What does the structure do with the Kaveri's water?
(b) What did this make possible for farming in the delta?
(c) How does (b) explain the name 'rice bowl of the South'?
(d) The Kallanai has been 'restored several times in the course of time'. What does this tell us about how later people valued it?
(e) Using what the chapter says about its present use, explain why it can be called a project 'for the benefit of the people' even today.
questions.a: (a) It diverts waters from the Kaveri to the central and southern parts of the Kaveri delta. (b) More land could be brought under cultivation. (c) With much more land farmed using the diverted water, the area became so productive that it earned the name 'rice bowl of the South'. (d) People found it worth repairing again and again instead of abandoning it, so they kept valuing it across many centuries. (e) It is still in use and helps millions of people in Tamil Nadu by providing water for irrigation and supporting agriculture, so its benefit reaches far beyond Karikala's own time.
s: States that it diverts Kaveri water to the central and southern delta
States that more land could be brought under cultivation
Links more cultivated land to the name 'rice bowl of the South'
Infers from repeated restoration that later people kept valuing it
Uses its present use for millions in Tamil Nadu to show lasting benefit

questions.q: Three classmates each claim that a different kingdom - the Cholas, the Cheras or the Pandyas - was the strongest in the south during this age. Give the best evidence from the chapter for each kingdom, choose a clear measure of 'strongest', and decide which kingdom your measure favours.
questions.a: Cholas: Karikala is said to have defeated a combined force of the Cheras and Pandyas and established his supremacy, and built the Kallanai. Cheras: their kingdom was a hub for exports of spices, timber, ivory and pearls to the Roman Empire and West Asia. Pandyas: Megasthenes describes a prosperous kingdom with a strong administration and active trade with the Greeks and Romans, and they were an important naval power. Measure and decision, for example: by military success the Cholas, since Karikala beat the other two together; by trade the Cheras or Pandyas could be argued. Any decision consistent with the chosen measure and the evidence earns the marks.
s: Chola evidence: Karikala's victory over the combined Chera-Pandya force
Chera evidence: hub of exports to Rome and West Asia
Pandya evidence: Megasthenes's prosperous, strongly administered kingdom and naval power
States a clear measure of 'strongest'
Reaches a decision consistent with the measure and the evidence

questions.q: The Heliodorus pillar, named after an Indo-Greek ambassador, stands near which place?
questions.a: Near Vidisha, in Madhya Pradesh.

questions.q: The Shaka Samvat is 78 years behind the Gregorian calendar, except from January to March, when it is behind by 79 years. A Government of India notice is dated 10 June 2029 in the Gregorian calendar. In which Shaka Samvat year was it issued?
questions.a: 1951: June is outside January-March, so the gap is 78 years, and 2029 - 78 = 1951.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Indo-Greeks and the Shakas.
I. The Shaka Samvat is 79 years behind the Gregorian calendar from April to December.
II. The Shakas ruled from the latter part of the 2nd century BCE to the 5th century CE.
III. Every Indo-Greek coin found shows an Indian deity such as Vasudeva-Krishna or Lakshmi.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only statement II is correct. Statement I is wrong: the gap is 78 years for most of the year and 79 only from January to March. Statement III is wrong: Indo-Greek coins often portrayed Greek deities; only some showed Indian deities.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Coins provide most of the information we have about the Indo-Greek rulers.
Reason (R): During excavations in north India, archaeologists have found many Indo-Greek coins.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: because so many Indo-Greek coins have been excavated in north India, they supply most of what we know about these rulers.

questions.q: True or False? 'The rule of the Indo-Greeks ended with the invasions of the Shakas, who are also called Indo-Scythians.' Give the verdict and say what ended the Shakas' own time in power.
questions.a: True. The Shakas (Indo-Scythians) ended Indo-Greek rule, and they in turn stayed in power until the arrival of the Kushanas.
s: States the verdict: True
States that the Shakas stayed in power until the Kushanas arrived

questions.q: Put these events in the order in which they happened, and explain the link between them. P: The Shakas end Indo-Greek rule in the northwest. Q: Satraps left behind by Alexander set up independent domains. R: The Kushanas arrive and the Shakas' time in power ends. S: After the decline of the Mauryas the northwest becomes an easy target for the Indo-Greeks.
questions.a: Order: Q, S, P, R. Alexander's satraps became independent rulers known as the Indo-Greeks; when the Mauryas declined, the weak northwest was an easy target and the Indo-Greeks took it; the Shakas' invasions then ended Indo-Greek rule; and the Shakas were in power until the Kushanas arrived.
s: Gives the order Q, S, P, R
Explains that the satraps became the Indo-Greeks, who took the weak northwest after the Maurya decline
Explains that the Shakas ended Indo-Greek rule and lasted until the Kushanas came

questions.q:
Ravi visits a museum gallery called 'Rulers from the Northwest'. Panel 1 tells how a conqueror retreating from the Indus plains left regional governors behind, who later set up independent domains. Panel 2 is a glass case of Indo-Greek coins made of four different metals, most with a king on one side and Greek deities on the other. Panel 3 is a map of a people, sometimes called Indo-Scythians, who invaded the northwest and ruled from the latter part of the 2nd century BCE to the 5th century CE, until the Kushanas arrived.
(a) What were the governors in Panel 1 called, and by what name did they later come to be known?
(b) Name the four metals of the coins in Panel 2.
(c) Name the people shown in Panel 3.
(d) Whose rule did the people in Panel 3 bring to an end?
questions.a: (a) Satraps; they came to be known as the Indo-Greeks. (b) Gold, silver, copper and nickel. (c) The Shakas. (d) The rule of the Indo-Greeks, which ended with the invasions of the Shakas.
s: Names satraps and Indo-Greeks
Names gold, silver, copper and nickel
Names the Shakas
States that they ended Indo-Greek rule

questions.q:
A class display on 'Greek and Indian cultures blending in the northwest' has three possible exhibits. Exhibit 1: an Indo-Greek silver coin with Vasudeva-Krishna on one side. Exhibit 2: the Heliodorus pillar near Vidisha. Exhibit 3: a Government of India publication dated in both the Gregorian and Shaka Samvat eras.
(a) What does Exhibit 1 show about blending?
(b) What does the inscription on Exhibit 2 show about the beliefs of the man it is named after?
(c) Why does Exhibit 3 not fit this display's theme, though it is a legacy of the same age?
(d) The chapter says the Indo-Greeks arrived as conquerors but were 'much influenced by the rich local culture'. In Exhibits 1 and 2, does the influence mainly flow from Greek to Indian or from Indian to Greek? Explain using both exhibits.
(e) Indo-Greek coins often portrayed Greek deities. Why does this not cancel the evidence of Exhibit 1?
questions.a: (a) A coin of an Indo-Greek ruler carries an Indian deity, so Indian religious ideas entered the coinage of rulers who came as conquerors. (b) Heliodorus, an Indo-Greek ambassador, praises Vasudeva as the 'god of gods', so he had taken up an Indian religious belief. (c) The Shaka Samvat was developed in the period of the Shakas (Indo-Scythians), who ended Indo-Greek rule; it shows the lasting legacy of the Shaka period, not blending between Greeks and Indians. (d) From Indian to Greek: in both exhibits it is people of Greek background who take up an Indian deity (an Indo-Greek ruler putting Vasudeva-Krishna on his coin, and an Indo-Greek ambassador praising Vasudeva), which matches the chapter's point that the conquerors were influenced by local culture. (e) A blend means Indian elements appeared alongside Greek ones, not that they replaced them; some coins showing Indian deities among many showing Greek deities is exactly what a blend looks like.
s: Explains that an Indian deity on an Indo-Greek coin shows Indian ideas entering their coinage
States that Heliodorus praised Vasudeva as the 'god of gods'
Explains that the Shaka Samvat is a Shaka legacy, not Greek-Indian blending
Says the influence flows from Indian to Greek, supported by both exhibits
Explains that blending means Indian elements alongside Greek ones, not replacing them

questions.q: Where did the Kushanas originally come from?
questions.a: Central Asia; they entered India probably in the 2nd century CE.

questions.q: A museum shows a sculpture of Kubera, the god of wealth, carved in red sandstone with a full, smoothly modelled body and a prominent moustache. To which school of art does it belong, and where did that school develop?
o: Mathura school, in present-day Uttar Pradesh
Gandhara school, in the western regions of Punjab
Mathura school, in the western regions of Punjab
Gandhara school, in present-day Uttar Pradesh
questions.a: The Mathura school, which developed in the Mathura region of present-day Uttar Pradesh, used red sandstone, produced fuller figures with smooth modelling and depicted Indian deities such as Kubera.

questions.q:
Match each item of the Kushana age in Column I with its description in Column II.
Column I: 1. Gandhara style  2. Mathura style  3. Silk Route  4. Kanishka's headless statue
Column II: P. Emerged in the Mathura region and mainly used red sandstone  Q. A trade network linking China with the Mediterranean world, large sections of it held by the Kushanas  R. A statue 1.85 m high with a Brahmi inscription giving royal titles  S. Emerged in the western regions of Punjab and used grey-black schist
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: Gandhara = western Punjab, grey-black schist; Mathura = Mathura region, red sandstone; Silk Route = trade network from China to the Mediterranean, largely held by the Kushanas; Kanishka's headless statue = 1.85 m high with a Brahmi inscription of his titles.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The age covered by this chapter saw the composition of major Indian texts such as the Mahabharata and the Ramayana.
Reason (R): The Kushanas held control over significant sections of the Silk Route.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: control of a trade route explains the growth of trade, not the composition of Sanskrit epics, which the chapter links to the flourishing of Sanskrit literature.

questions.q: True or False? 'At its peak, the Kushana empire extended from central Asia to large parts of northern India.' Give the verdict and name the ruler the chapter calls probably the most powerful of the dynasty.
questions.a: True. At its peak the Kushana empire stretched from central Asia to large parts of northern India; Kanishka was probably its most powerful ruler.
s: States the verdict: True
Names Kanishka as probably the most powerful Kushana ruler

questions.q: (a) In the Kushana age, how did the way deities such as Surya were shown begin to change? (b) What did the growth of religious art in this era lay the groundwork for?
questions.a: (a) Deities came to be represented looking more similar to humans. (b) It laid the groundwork for later temple architecture in the subcontinent.
s: States that deities began to be shown looking more like humans
States that it laid the groundwork for later temple architecture

questions.q: Give three differences between the Gandhara and Mathura schools of art: (a) the region where each developed, (b) the stone each mainly used, (c) how much Greco-Roman influence each shows.
questions.a: (a) Gandhara emerged in the western regions of Punjab; Mathura developed in the Mathura region of present-day Uttar Pradesh. (b) Gandhara mainly used grey-black schist; Mathura mainly used red sandstone. (c) Gandhara blended Greco-Roman elements with Indian features; Mathura has a distinct Indian style with less Greco-Roman influence.
s: Gives the regions: western Punjab against the Mathura region of Uttar Pradesh
Gives the stones: grey-black schist against red sandstone
Contrasts the influence: Greco-Roman blend in Gandhara, less of it in Mathura

questions.q: The chapter says that Kushana art continued 'the trend set under the Indo-Greek rulers'. Explain this with three points: what the trend was under the Indo-Greeks, how Kushana-age art carried it on, and one Kushana coin that shows the same mixing.
questions.a: Under the Indo-Greeks, Greek and Indian elements blended in governance, art, language and daily life. Kushana art, in the Gandhara and Mathura schools, is celebrated for its fusion of Indian and Greek styles, with Gandhara blending Greco-Roman elements with Indian features. One of Kanishka's coins shows the Buddha with his name written in Greek script (BODDO).
s: Describes the Indo-Greek blending of Greek and Indian elements
Explains the Gandhara and Mathura fusion of Indian and Greek styles
Cites Kanishka's coin with the Buddha named in Greek script

questions.q:
A school museum club is lent a box of 60 coins of a powerful ruler of a dynasty from central Asia. On 25 coins the ruler holds a spear on one side, and the other side shows the Buddha with his name written in a foreign script. On 20 coins the other side shows Shiva with the bull Nandi. The remaining 15 show other figures. The club must give its display one of two titles: 'A Buddhist King' or 'Many Faiths on One Coinage'.
(a) Name the ruler and the script in which the Buddha's name is written.
(b) What percentage of the 60 coins show either the Buddha or Shiva?
(c) What does a ruler putting both the Buddha and Shiva on his coins suggest about his values?
(d) Which title should the club choose? Justify using (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) Kanishka; Greek script. (b) 25 + 20 = 45 of 60 = 75%. (c) He honoured more than one school of thought, in line with the chapter's picture of the peaceful co-existence of various schools. (d) 'Many Faiths on One Coinage': although the Buddha coins (25) are a little more numerous, 20 of the 45 show Shiva, so the coinage does not show one faith alone.
s: Names Kanishka and the Greek script
Computes 45 of 60 = 75%
Infers respect for more than one school of thought
Chooses 'Many Faiths on One Coinage' and justifies it with the Buddha and Shiva counts

questions.q: 'Despite political conflicts and power struggles, the age of reorganisation was an age of cultural confluence.' Do you agree? Support your view with four pieces of evidence from different peoples or schools in the chapter, and then give your overall judgement.
questions.a: Evidence: (1) The Indo-Greeks, though they came as conquerors, blended Greek and Indian elements, and the Indo-Greek ambassador Heliodorus praised Vasudeva as the 'god of gods'. (2) Some Indo-Greek coins showed Indian deities like Vasudeva-Krishna and Lakshmi. (3) Kanishka's coins show the Buddha named in Greek script, and Shiva with Nandi. (4) The Gandhara school blended Greco-Roman elements with Indian features, while Kushana-age sculpture showed a variety of deities. Judgement: agree; the chapter says the period saw remarkable cultural exchange and assimilation, with styles interacting but with a dominance of Indian themes and a flourishing of Sanskrit literature.
s: Evidence from the Indo-Greeks: blending, or Heliodorus praising Vasudeva
Evidence from Indo-Greek coins with Indian deities
Evidence from Kanishka's coins with the Buddha in Greek script and Shiva
Evidence from Gandhara or Mathura art
Overall judgement noting exchange with a dominance of Indian themes
